standard.title: Values, Social Cohesion and Democracy
standard.description: how values based on freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity can support social cohesion and democracy within Australian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand Australia's democratic freedoms and the characteristics of active and formal citizenship (AC9HC7K02). They have explored Australia's pluralist, multi-faith society and diverse cultural origins (AC9HC7K04). This descriptor extends that to examine how shared values can hold a diverse society together.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how values based on freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity can support social cohesion and democracy, evaluating the extent to which these values are reflected in Australian society.

nodes.label: Australian values and their expression
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify Australian values including freedom, respect, fairness, equality, compassion, and a 'fair go', and explain how these values are expressed through customs, protocols, and civic life.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least four Australian values (e.g. freedom, fairness, equality, a 'fair go') and describe one way each is expressed in Australian public or civic life.
nodes.typical_width: Identify a range of Australian values including patriotism, inclusion, civility, personal and collective responsibility, compassion, equality, justice, a 'fair go', and religious freedom; explain how these values are expressed through customs and protocols such as flag-raising ceremonies and the national anthem; investigate the history of changes to the national anthem.
wider: Investigate how the concept of a 'fair go' has been interpreted differently by different groups in Australian society, including debates about whether it is a lived reality or an aspiration
Explore how shared values can be expressed differently across cultural communities in Australia — examining how the same value manifests in different traditions
Compare Australian civic values with those articulated in national identity documents from other countries (e.g. the US Declaration of Independence, the French Republic's motto)

response_modes.reason: Students need to build a genuine repertoire of Australian civic values with concrete examples — this is the factual foundation before evaluating how well values are upheld.

success_criteria: Identify at least four Australian civic values and explain what each means
Describe at least one way Australian values are expressed through public customs or protocols

nodes.label: Values and social cohesion
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how shared values can promote social cohesion and reconciliation in Australia's diverse society, and evaluate the extent to which these values are reflected in Australian society.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what 'social cohesion' means and identify at least one way shared values (e.g. fairness, inclusion) support people from diverse backgrounds living together in Australian society.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how shared values support social cohesion in a diverse society; evaluate the extent to which values like freedom, respect, fairness and equality are genuinely reflected in Australian society, including examining where gaps between aspiration and reality exist; consider how these values can promote reconciliation.
wider: Evaluate the extent to which Australian values are reflected across different groups — examining evidence of inequality, discrimination or exclusion that challenges claims about shared values

Investigate how reconciliation between First Nations and non-Indigenous Australians is understood as a values-driven process, and examine specific initiatives (e.g. Sorry Day, Reconciliation Action Plans)
Explore how migrants and refugees experience Australian values when arriving in Australia — what aspects of Australian civic life help or hinder their participation
nodes.hinge_reason: The evaluation of whether values are actually reflected in society — not just stated — is the conceptual core of this descriptor. Students who only identify values without evaluating their application cannot meet the descriptor's command term ('can support') which implies a conditional, evaluative claim.

response_modes.reason: Evaluating the gap between stated values and lived reality requires careful reasoning — students need a scaffold for assessing evidence of both alignment and failure, and for making conditional claims about what values 'can' (but do not always) achieve.

Reconciliation as a values-driven process offers rich context for exploring how social cohesion is actively built rather than passively assumed — examine specific initiatives alongside the ongoing gaps.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Reconciliation as a case study connects values to real political and social processes in Australia, giving students a meaningful context for evaluating whether and how shared values can bridge historical division — this is among the most significant contemporary civic issues in Australia.
success_criteria: Explain what social cohesion means and identify how shared values support it in a diverse society
Evaluate at least one area where Australian values are strongly reflected and one area where there is a gap between aspiration and reality

nodes.label: Religious and Christian traditions in Australian society
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify Christian traditions and values that have influenced the development of Australian society, democracy and law, and identify the values and beliefs of other religions practised in contemporary Australia.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two Christian traditions or values that have shaped Australian society, democracy or law, and name at least two other religions practised in contemporary Australia.
nodes.typical_width: Identify Christian traditions and values that have influenced Australian society, democracy and law (including impacts on First Nations communities and other groups); identify the values and beliefs of religions practised in contemporary Australia such as Judaism, Buddhism, Islam and Hinduism.
wider: Investigate the influence of Christian social teaching on Australian social policy areas such as healthcare, education and welfare, tracing connections to current institutions
Compare the core values and beliefs of two or more religions practised in Australia to identify areas of common ground and difference
Explore how religious diversity in Australia is managed through legal protections (freedom of religion) and social norms of tolerance, and examine cases where religious freedom has been contested

response_modes.reason: Comparative engagement with multiple religious traditions (not just naming them) helps students genuinely understand pluralism rather than just identifying diversity as a list.

success_criteria: Identify at least two Christian traditions that have shaped Australian society or law
Name at least two other religions practised in contemporary Australia and describe one key value or belief of each

nodes.label: Migrants, refugees and Australian values
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why migrants and refugees choose to come to Australia, connecting this to the values and freedoms that characterise Australian society.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two reasons why people choose to migrate to or seek refuge in Australia, connecting at least one to Australian democratic values or freedoms.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate why migrants and refugees wish to come to Australia and become Australian citizens; explain how Australian values (freedom, safety, rule of law, opportunity) attract people from other countries; evaluate how the reality of life in Australia aligns with migrants' and refugees' expectations.
wider: Investigate the experiences of refugees from a specific country of origin, examining what they are seeking in Australia and how well Australia's values and systems meet those needs
Explore the citizenship process and what obligations and rights come with Australian citizenship, connecting this to the values underpinning citizenship
Examine debates in Australia about immigration and refugee policy, connecting these to values of fairness, compassion, and security to analyse competing value claims

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the earlier examination of Australian values with a perspective from outside — people choosing Australia connects the values to their lived attractiveness and tests whether values are genuinely reflected in Australian life.

success_criteria: Identify at least two reasons why people choose to migrate to Australia and connect at least one to Australian democratic values
Explain how Australian values and freedoms are relevant to the decisions migrants and refugees make
